Hi Sam — quick answers and a practical checklist you can use during the first sprint.

Token rotation: Redwood supports short-lived keys via our token service (recommended). We provide a refresh endpoint that your proxy can call; alternately you can use your own rotating proxy. For production we recommend 15m–1h TTL with server-side refresh to avoid client exposure.

Test dataset: a 5–10k row de-identified CSV/NDJSON is ideal for sampling latency and batch embeddings. If you want to test streaming latency, include ~50 longer prompts (~1–2k tokens).

SDK setup (examples):
- curl quick test (staging):
  curl -X POST https://staging.api.redwood.com/v1/generate 
    -H 'Authorization: Bearer REPLACE_ME' 
    -H 'Content-Type: application/json' 
    -d '{"model":"redwood-llm-small","input":"hello"}'

- Node SDK snippet (recommended retry/backoff defaults):
  const client = new Redwood({ apiKey: process.env.REDWOOD_KEY });
  // timeouts in ms, retries with jitter
  client.config({ timeout: 10000, retries: 3, backoffBase: 200, backoffCap: 2000 });
  const res = await client.generate({ model: 'redwood-llm-small', input: 'ping' });

Retries/Timeouts guidance:
- Client timeout: 8–12s per token-run for interactive endpoints; 30–60s for long-batch jobs.
- Retries: use idempotency keys for generate requests if you plan retries on 5xx or network errors. 3 attempts with exponential jitter (200ms -> 800ms -> 2s) works well.
- Backoff: respect Retry-After header when present. If 429, prefer linear backoff + queueing on your side.

Rate-limit handling:
- Redwood returns X-RateLimit-Limit, X-RateLimit-Remaining, X-RateLimit-Reset. Monitor Remaining and implement client-side token bucket.
- For bursty workloads, request a short burst quota during cutover; we can coordinate a temporary increase for the canary window (requires pre-approval).

Endpoint migration plan (recommended minimal steps):
1) Mirror calls to staging and collect telemetry for 24–48h.
2) Canary: route 1–2% traffic to Redwood staging with app-level circuit breaker.
3) Gradual ramp: 10% -> 50% -> 100% across 24–72h observing latency and error budget.
4) Rollback plan: immediate 100% fallback to old endpoint on error rate > 1% or latency degradation > 2x.

Attachments: env-template.env (sample env vars), small README in sdk-sample-snippets.zip with full examples.

- Monica Patel

Hi all — a couple of operational notes to add before the kickoff: 

Monitoring & observability:
- Instrument request_id across the call chain (Redwood returns request-id in X-Request-Id).
- Add a lightweight tracer for the first 48 hours of canary traffic to detect tail-latency.

Traffic shaping during cutover:
- If you have time-based spikes (EOD batch jobs), exclude those windows from the initial ramp or run them at reduced concurrency.
- Use a token bucket client to smooth bursts; server-side we can enable short prefix caching for repeated prompts to reduce cost and latency.

Quota & SLA notes:
- I'll request a temporary burst quota for the canary (requires signature on the short MOU). If you need higher burst capacity please share expected rps and average tokens per minute.

Operational checklist for kickoff (we'll bring infra on the call):
- Confirm test keys and rotation plan
- Confirm logging (sample log format)
- Agree canary gating metrics and rollback thresholds

I'll drop a brief runbook in the Drive link before the call.

— Vivek Kulkarni
Platform Ops | Redwood Inference
